analysis:
This PR contains only documentation and a changelog entry. The changelog (changelog.d/provider-disconnected-chunk-drop.md, lines 1-4) and the new paragraph in docs/architecture/inference.md (head lines 1287-1300) describe a code change in ChunkBatcher.enqueue that is not in the supplied evidence. As described, response frames processed on the serial queue while no session sink is bound are dropped immediately, so a deferred flush cannot deliver them to a replacement session after reconnect. Because the Swift source is not supplied, I cannot verify that behavior; I treat it as a described control, not a verified one.

Relevant threats: T-008 and TB-002 (response frames and ciphertext reaching the wrong session after reconnect), A-001 (prompt/completion confidentiality), and T-010 (cancellation on teardown). The described change appears to narrow stale-frame delivery. The doc is also candid about a residual gap: SendHandle and ChunkSender persist across reconnects, so a frame from an old request that is processed after a replacement sink binds still passes the sink check. The code does not enforce request-to-session identity. ProviderLoop+Cancellation.swift cancels in-flight requests separately. Frames are end-to-end encrypted per request to the coordinator hop, and the coordinator is trusted and rejects unknown request IDs. The stale-frame path therefore looks like a correctness or integrity concern rather than a confirmed disclosure. This is not a regression introduced by the diff.

No security regression is identifiable from the docs alone, and no threat-model assumption is invalidated. The next review pass should examine the following in the real code: (1) ChunkBatcher.swift, to confirm that the sink check runs on the queue and that a pending buffer is cleared on unbind; (2) CoordinatorClient+Connection.swift teardown ordering versus rebind; (3) whether the coordinator ignores or rejects chunks for request IDs it did not issue on that session; and (4) the SendHandle.send terminal flush path.
